title: Too Much, Too Soon
author: Andrew Cantarutti
summary: Part 2 of a series on attention as curriculum contrasts two ten-year-olds twenty years apart: one who earned independence in small, deliberate increments, and one handed a smartphone and an unbounded digital world before his executive attention had developed. Drawing on the Rothbart-Posner three-network model of attention, the piece lays out what schools should (and shouldn't) teach about attention at each developmental stage, from 'conditions, not content' in early childhood to naming manipulative design mechanisms in adolescence.
points: Contrasts 'Max' (2006), who earned independence through deliberate increments like solo errands, with 'Oliver' (2026), whose first taste of independence was an unsupervised smartphone.
Rothbart and Posner's three-network model (alerting, orienting, executive attention) shows executive attention develops last and needs less stimulation, not more.
In early childhood (0-7), schools and families should provide conditions — unstructured play, minimal screens — not direct instruction in attention.
In middle childhood (7-11), kids develop 'retrospective monitoring,' making it possible to teach them to recognize and redirect their own wandering attention.
Only in adolescence (12+) can students grasp that attention is deliberately captured by systems built by people with financial incentives — the 'naming the mechanism' stage.
quotes: Nobody told Max that fetching items off a list was training his sustained attention
Max was rewarded with more independence on his tenth birthday. Oliver was given his first iPhone.
Executive attention needs less stimulation to develop well, not more.
The developmental window that sharpens our executive attention is widest in early childhood, but it continues to improve through adolescence.
Adolescents can begin to understand things like revenue and the incentives that spur design decisions.
